# Continuous pulse oximetry monitoring in children hospitalized with bronchiolitis: a qualitative analysis of clinicians’ justifications

**Authors:** Halley Ruppel; Christopher P. Bonafide; Rinad S. Beidas; Kimberly Albanowski; Raymond Parlar-Chun; Prabi Rajbhandari; Andrew S. Kern-Goldberger; Patricia A. Stoeck; Kathleen Snow; Samantha A. House; Kate E. Lucey; Patrick W. Brady; Amanda C. Schondelmeyer

## Abstract

Continuous pulse oximetry monitoring use outside established guidelines is common in children hospitalized with bronchiolitis. We analyzed clinicians’ real time rationale for continuous monitoring in stable children with bronchiolitis not requiring supplemental oxygen. Data for this study were collected as part a multi-center deimplementation trial for continuous pulse oximetry in children hospitalized with bronchiolitis. We analyzed 371 clinician responses across 36 hospitals; 258 (70%) responses did not include a clinical reason for monitoring (“non-clinical”; e.g., respondent forgot to discontinue monitoring, did not know why the patient was monitored, or was following an order). The remaining 113 (30%) responses contained a clinical reason for monitoring (“clinical”; e.g., recently requiring oxygen, physical exam concerns, or concerns relating to patient condition or history). Strategies to reduce unnecessary monitoring should include changes in workflow to facilitate shared understanding of monitoring goals and timely discontinuation of monitoring.

## Introduction

Children hospitalized with bronchiolitis are frequently placed on continuous pulse oximetry (cSpO2) monitoring. Guidelines recommend using intermittent pulse oximetry (“spot checks”) rather than cSpO2 monitoring in these patients when not receiving supplemental oxygen (“in room air”).1,2 Unnecessary cSpO2 monitoring may result in more harm than benefit by, for example, increasing length of stay or eliciting excessive intervention.3,4 Still, nearly half of bronchiolitis patients not receiving supplemental oxygen may be cSpO2 monitored.5

Understanding clinician decision-making surrounding the use of continuous physiologic monitoring, including cSpO2, in children is limited. A few interview studies have explored clinicians’ rationales for continuous monitoring of heart rate, respiratory rate, or SpO2 in hospitalized children; common themes include clinician or parental comfort when the patient is continuously monitored.6–8 However, these relatively small studies relied on clinicians to recall “work as done”9 during interviews, which may be subject to memory limitations or cognitive biases. We therefore sought to analyze reasons for using cSpO2 monitoring in children with stable bronchiolitis in room air as reported by clinicians while actively providing patient care. The results of this granular analysis can be used to inform strategies to ensure intentional monitoring aligned with evidence and guidelines.

## Methods

We conducted a descriptive qualitative study10 of open-ended responses from clinicians obtained as part of an audit and feedback strategy within the Eliminating Monitor Overuse (EMO) trial, a multi-center hybrid effectiveness-deimplementation trial focused on cSpO2 monitoring in children hospitalized with bronchiolitis.11 The EMO trial compared the effects of different strategies on sustained deimplementation of cSpO2 in children hospitalized with bronchiolitis in room air.

During the trial’s active deimplementation phase, research staff from hospitals in both study arms (n=36) collected data on oxygen use and monitoring status of patients aged 2–23 months with bronchiolitis, no major comorbidities, and born at ≥28 weeks gestation, using a convenience sampling approach.11 As part of the audit and feedback strategies conducted across all hospitals (regardless of study arm), study staff conducted Real Time Inquiry (RTI) for patients without supplemental oxygen or flow, but who were on cSpO2 monitoring. The RTI process involved study team members at each site approaching member(s) of the healthcare team (e.g., resident, nurse, attending) in a non-confrontational manner, either in person or via secure messaging, to ask about the rationale for cSpO2 monitoring (e.g., “Can you tell me why the patient is still continuously monitored with pulse oximetry?”). Study staff were instructed to approach any available member of the healthcare team for RTI when convenient during data collection. Staff recorded the respondent’s role and their verbatim or paraphrased response.

We used descriptive statistics to summarize RTI data by site and clinician type. Two investigators (HR, AS) conducted qualitative analysis of the responses. They independently inductively coded a subset of 40 responses before coming together to develop and refine a series of categories to group and describe the justifications for cSpO2 monitoring. These investigators then independently coded all responses and iteratively conferred, coming to agreement on all decisions. In instances where two categories might apply, the coding team reached consensus on the most appropriate category, such that categories were mutually exclusive. Categories were further collapsed, refined, and defined in collaboration with the study team.

## Results

Of 2052 patients not receiving any supplemental oxygen or flow for ≥1 hour, 520 (25%) were on cSpO2 monitoring. EMO team members conducted RTI in a convenience sample of 384 of the 520 (74%), with a median of 8.5 RTIs per site (IQR 3.75–15). Most commonly, RTI was conducted with a nurse (n=290, 76%), followed by a resident trainee (n=56, 15%), attending physician (n=17, 4%), multidisciplinary group (n=12, 3%), advanced practice provider (n=6, 2%), or respiratory therapist (n=3, 1%). For qualitative analysis, we excluded 13 (3%) RTIs where the recorded response did not include a clear rationale (e.g., “message sent to RN with no response”, “no reply given”; Figure).

We categorized the remaining 371 responses into non-clinical and clinical responses. Subcategories, definitions, and example responses can be found in the Table. We categorized most responses as non-clinical, as the primary justification provided did not include a specific clinical concern (n=258, 70%). Non-clinical responses were the most common type of response for nurses (198/290, 68%) and residents/advanced practice providers (38/62, 61%). Of the non-clinical responses, the highest proportion were instances in which the clinician stated they forgot or had not had time to discontinue monitoring (n=71, 28%). In another 20%, the clinician did not know the reason for monitoring or stated the monitor had been left on by a previous provider (“already on”) (n=52). Responses were categorized as “clinical” when they included any clinical justification for monitoring, without evaluation of the soundness of the rationale. Of the clinical reasons given for monitoring (n=113, 30%), the largest proportion related to recently requiring oxygen or doing a “room air challenge” or “nap test” (n=50, 44%). Other common clinical reasons included physical exam concerns (e.g., desaturations) (n=35, 31%), or concerns about patient history, such as chronic illness or age (n=19, 17%).

## Discussion

Among children hospitalized with bronchiolitis in 36 hospitals, the most common rationales provided by clinicians for cSpO2 monitoring in the absence of supplemental oxygen reflected non-clinical reasoning—such as forgetting to discontinue monitoring when no longer needed or not knowing the reason for monitoring. The most common clinical reasons provided for cSpO2 monitoring included recent supplemental oxygen requirement and physical exam concerns.

Our results confirmed previous findings that family preferences and individual clinician comfort influence decisions to continuously monitor hospitalized children.6–8 However, these factors were brought up in a smaller number of responses compared with forgetting or lacking time to remove the monitor. By inquiring about monitoring reasons in real time, we may have captured reasons for cSpO2 monitoring that clinicians do not recall or disclose in interviews conducted outside of the clinical setting. Our findings of forgetting or lacking time to remove monitoring may indicate that busy clinicians do not prioritize promptly discontinuing monitoring when no longer clinically indicated, which is consistent with findings by Yama et al.8

Continuing unnecessary monitoring is not without risks. Studies have demonstrated that even brief periods of monitoring in patients who are clinically improving can contribute to high alarm rates,12 which have been linked to increased nurse workload13 and prolonged response times.14 Along with our findings, these results suggest strategies aimed at standardizing aspects of workflow for timely discontinuation of monitors would be high-yield for reducing unnecessary alarms on general hospital medicine units, which care for a disproportionate number of children with bronchiolitis during seasonal surges of respiratory viruses.

Our finding that many clinicians did not know why patients in their care were monitored also suggests a potential lack of shared situation awareness among team members regarding the use of cSpO2 monitoring. Other studies have suggested that team communication and decision making around continuous monitoring are important but often lacking.6,8 Future strategies to reduce over-monitoring could include workflow changes that facilitate: (1) shared understanding of monitoring purpose and status, and (2) timely discontinuation of monitors when no longer clinically warranted. Promising potential strategies include incorporating monitoring into formal communication events, like hand off and rounds; discontinuation of monitoring orders by members of the healthcare team other than physicians; and electronic-health record order sets and alerts that facilitate shared awareness of monitoring status and evidence-based guidelines.7

Many of the clinical responses were vague or not grounded in guideline or evidence-based practice (e.g., “room air challenge” and “nap tests”). Although this could indicate a knowledge gap, these responses also reflect seeking a sense of comfort or reassurance from continued cSpO2 monitoring. Seeking reassurance from cSpO2 monitoring may indicate distrust in other components of the patient monitoring system—such as regular assessment by clinicians—to adequately detect and prevent deterioration. While educational strategies may help reduce parents’ desire for cSpO2 monitoring,15 future research should explore the source of clinicians’ concerns about unmonitored children on medical-surgical units. In a few cases, clinicians reported that they were monitoring simply because no one was at the bedside, which may reflect safety concerns related to hazards of the hospital environment (e.g., falls or risk for injury from tubing and cords).

Strengths of this study include responses from a diverse set of hospitals, use of RTI, and use of a standard definition of monitoring overuse derived from prior national guidelines. However, our findings should be considered in light of limitations related to our methods. First, because data collectors included clinicians, respondents may have been influenced to provide responses they perceived to be socially desirable. Most hospitals included in the study were free-standing children’s hospitals. Clinicians’ monitoring practices and perspectives may differ in other settings. For example, in community settings with fewer pediatric trained staff, clinical concerns may be more prevalent. Furthermore, we included responses from a heterogeneous group of clinicians, although most respondents were nurses. Including responses from only nurses or only physicians may have resulted in different findings. While nurses tend to have a more up-to-date assessment of the patient, physicians or advanced practice providers order monitoring in most institutions. In a few cases, data collectors actually recorded different reasons for monitoring from different members of the clinical team. Because the data collectors were not consistently asking multiple members of the team for a response, we could not accurately quantify discordance among team members. Finally, coding of responses required team member judgment when multiple reasons for monitoring were provided or multiple subcategories were applicable. Because of the relative brevity of responses, it was not always easy to tease apart rationales, resulting in categories that grouped rationales that may require different solutions (e.g., Forgot/No Time; Don’t Know/Monitor Already On).

In conclusion, for hospitalized children with bronchiolitis in room air, clinicians most often provided non-clinical reasons for ongoing, guideline-discordant cSpO2 monitoring. Standardized processes that support timely discontinuation of monitoring in eligible patients may further reduce unnecessary monitoring.
